prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
There is an obvious version of distraction: a notification arrives, you look at your phone, and your attention moves. But research has found a quieter version. Your eyes can stay on the task, and the phone can remain untouched, yet your performance can still change.

One study tested 73 university students in 960 short visual trials. Some trials included a notification sound. Others included a neutral sound. The students did not look at or touch a phone. Even so, their responses were slower when the notification sound played.

A second study showed a different version of the same problem. Forty-two university students took an attention test. A powered-off phone was either on the desk or in another room. No notification arrived in either condition. Attention and processing-speed scores were lower when the phone stayed on the desk.

The experience also appears in daily life. In a 2018 survey of 743 U.S. teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications before doing much else after waking.

When their phone was not with them, 56% reported at least one of three feelings: anxiety, loneliness, or being upset. Smaller shares reported each feeling individually. A majority also said they felt a need to answer texts, social-media messages, and other notifications quickly.

Together, these findings show two quiet interruptions: one begins with a sound, and one appears when the phone is simply present. The survey does not prove that the phone caused the reported feelings. But it shows why the lab results connect with a familiar daily experience.

【Point One】
The first study reveals a hidden layer. The notification condition also produced a larger N2 signal in the brain-wave recording. Researchers interpret this as extra control resources being used to keep the task going. So a person may keep looking at the screen and still pay a mental cost. “I did not check my phone” does not mean “it had no effect.”

【Point Two】
The second study points to a different lever: location. Among 42 students, attention scores were about 100 with a powered-off phone on the desk, versus about 109 when it was in another room. Processing speed showed the same pattern: it was lower when the phone was on the desk. No notification arrived in either condition. Moving a phone out of the workspace is therefore a different choice from simply silencing or powering it off.

point_one.reasoning: Full Storyの反応時間の低下に加え、通知音でN2信号が大きくなり、課題を続けるための認知的制御資源が余分に使われたというメカニズムを示している。「確認していなくても精神的コストが生じる」という具体的な示唆があり、新しい価値を加えている。

point_two.reasoning: Full Storyにない具体的なスコア（机上約100、別室約109）を示し、通知の有無ではなく端末の位置が注意力に関わる別の介入点だと明確化している。消音・電源オフだけでなく作業場所から移すという実践的な選択肢を提示しており、理解と行動上の示唆を深めている。
